content: Virtual reality (VR) technology creates a simulated environment that users can actively interact with, and it is perceived as comparable to the real world. The effectiveness of VR as a distraction technique for reducing acute pain intensity in children remains uncertain. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and potential adverse effects of VR distraction interventions for children aged 0 to 18 years experiencing acute pain in healthcare settings. To gather evidence, databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and four trial registries were searched up to October 2019. Additional sources included reference lists of eligible studies, handsearching relevant journals, and contacting study authors. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including cross-over and cluster RCTs, that compared VR distraction to no distraction, non-VR distraction, or other VR distraction methods. The primary outcome of interest was acute pain intensity, measured during procedures and up to one hour post-procedure. Secondary outcomes included adverse effects, child satisfaction with VR, pain-related distress, parent anxiety, use of rescue analgesia, and cost. Standard Cochrane methodological processes were used, with two reviewers independently assessing the risk of bias and extracting data. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, and summary tables were created. Seventeen RCTs involving 1008 participants aged 4 to 18 years were included. These studies involved various healthcare procedures, such as phlebotomy, burn wound dressings, and physical therapy sessions. Due to significant heterogeneity in the populations, procedural conditions, and pain levels, statistical pooling of data was not possible. Instead, the results were described narratively. Most studies were judged to have an unclear risk of selection bias, a high risk of performance and detection bias, and a high risk of bias due to small sample sizes. The certainty of evidence was downgraded to low or very low due to serious study limitations, indirectness, and imprecision. VR Distraction vs. No Distraction 1. Acute Pain Intensity During Procedures: Self-reported pain: One study (42 participants) found no beneficial effect of non-immersive VR (very low-certainty evidence). Observer-reported pain: No data available. Behavioral measurements (observer-reported): Two studies (62 participants) provided low-certainty evidence. One study (42 participants) found no beneficial effect of non-immersive VR, while another study (20 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR. 2. Acute Pain Intensity Post-Procedure: Self-reported pain: Ten studies (461 participants) provided very low-certainty evidence. Four studies (95 participants) found no beneficial effect of immersive, semi-immersive, or non-immersive VR. Five studies (357 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR. Another study (9 participants) reported less pain in the VR group. Observer-reported pain: Two studies (216 participants) provided low-certainty evidence. Both studies found a beneficial effect of immersive VR, as reported by caregivers, parents, or nurses. One study (80 participants) also found a beneficial effect as reported by researchers. Behavioral measurements (observer-reported): One study (42 participants) found no beneficial effect of non-immersive VR (very low-certainty evidence). 3. Adverse Effects: Five studies (154 participants) provided very low-certainty evidence. Three studies (53 participants) reported no adverse effects. Two studies (101 participants) reported mild adverse effects, such as nausea, in the VR group. VR Distraction vs. Non-VR Distraction 1. Acute Pain Intensity During Procedures: Self-reported pain: Two studies (106 participants) provided very low-certainty evidence. One study (65 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR, while another study (41 participants) found no evidence of a difference in mean pain change scores. Observer-reported pain: Two studies (106 participants) provided low-certainty evidence. One study (65 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR, while another study (41 participants) found no evidence of a difference in mean pain change scores. Behavioral measurements (observer-reported): Two studies (106 participants) provided low-certainty evidence. One study (65 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR, while another study (41 participants) reported fewer pain behaviors in the VR group. 2. Acute Pain Intensity Post-Procedure: Self-reported pain: Eight studies (575 participants) provided very low-certainty evidence. Two studies (146 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR. Two studies (252 participants) reported a between-group difference favoring immersive VR. One study (59 participants) found no beneficial effect of immersive VR compared to television and Child Life non-VR distraction. One study (18 participants) found no beneficial effect of semi-immersive VR. Two studies (100 participants) reported no between-group difference. Observer-reported pain: Three studies (187 participants) provided low-certainty evidence. One study (81 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR for parent, nurse, and researcher reports. Another study (65 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR for caregiver reports. A third study (41 participants) found no evidence of a difference in mean pain change scores. Behavioral measurements (observer-reported): Two studies (106 participants) provided low-certainty evidence. One study (65 participants) found a beneficial effect favoring immersive VR, while another study (41 participants) found no evidence of a difference in mean pain change scores. 3. Adverse Effects: Six studies (429 participants) provided very low-certainty evidence. Three studies (229 participants) found no evidence of a difference between groups. Two studies (141 participants) reported no adverse effects in the VR group. One study (59 participants) found no beneficial effect in reducing estimated cyber-sickness before and after VR immersion. VR Distraction vs. Other VR Distraction No studies were identified for this comparison. Authors' Conclusions The evidence for the effectiveness of VR distraction in reducing acute pain intensity in children is of low or very low certainty. This uncertainty makes it challenging to determine the benefits or lack thereof of VR distraction for acute pain management in children. Most primary outcomes were assessed by only two or three small studies, and data on adverse effects and secondary outcomes were limited. Future well-designed, large, high-quality trials are needed to improve confidence in the results.
